name: Elena Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the regional warehouse for a farm and garden supplies chain, about twenty minutes outside our town. We send out everything from chicken feed to fence posts to the shops. I pick small items, like gloves, seed packets and hose fittings, into crates, and I help load the lorries in the afternoon. I've been there just over a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The scanner wears me out, honestly. I'm not good with it, and I still write my pick list on paper as a backup, which my supervisor Dave teases me about. I like the people, most are local, and the radio's always on. My fiancé Mark works at the sawmill, and we're getting married next summer at our church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. People should work for a living, not have a computer do it. At church, people would nod along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a relief, mostly. But my worries were never about AI. They're about the wedding, the rent, and the fact that I've hardly anything saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, and maybe ask Dave for extra loading shifts in the run-up to spring, when the garden stuff goes out. Mark and I would trim the wedding, maybe skip the band and have my uncle do music. We'd keep to the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier, but still worried. Money's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding. How's the money for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. My mum's helping with the dress, and Mark's parents are paying for the hall. We'd be saving the rest from our wages, but there isn't much rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How's the sawmill doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. My fiancé Mark's sawmill has had him on four days since the summer. Mark doesn't complain, but I see him checking the bank app at night.

I never **trusted AI** anyway, and people at church would agree.
think: My worries were never AI; they're about the **wedding** and **rent**.
I've **hardly anything saved**, and that doesn't change.
do: Ask Dave for **extra loading shifts** before the spring garden rush.
**Trim the wedding**, skipping the band and asking my uncle to play.
feel: **Steadier**, but still worried, because money's money.

fieldNote: Her **pre-existing pressures** are a wedding, rent, thin savings and her fiancé's short time.
She values **work and family** and sees AI as something she never trusted.
She **resists technology**, still writing pick lists on paper.

steps.text: Ask Dave for extra loading shifts before the spring garden rush
Skip the wedding band and have her uncle play music

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but companies have to compete. I'd hope they'd look after the people who've been loyal. At church, we'd pray for those who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It worries me. I'm slow on the scanner, I'm new, and I can't see them keeping me if a computer does the planning and a robot loads the lorries. The thinking stuff won't touch my hands much yet, but it'll decide who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder. I'd talk to Mark about a smaller wedding, just family at the church and a meal after. I'd ask my dad whether there's work on my uncle's farm, if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I'm standing on a floor that might give way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My parents, then Mark's. And the church, the pastor's wife always knows who's hiring. Not the government, I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dave made me, yes. But I'd hate it, and I'd be slow. I'm better with my hands than screens.

At church we'd **pray** for those who lose work.
think: I'm **slow and new**, so I can't see them keeping me.

do: Plan a **smaller wedding**, just family at the church and a meal after.

Keep my head down and **work harder**.

fieldNote: She turns to **family and church**, refusing government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far, too fast. Somebody should have slowed it down. I'm not usually one for rules, but this is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd do. I'd lose the warehouse job, and maybe Mark loses the sawmill too. We'd have no savings, no plan, no idea what jobs there'd even be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Postpone the wedding, I suppose. Move back in with my parents. Pray a lot. I wouldn't know where to start with anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. My heart is going just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the thinking side changes in 2028 and robots for hands-on work come around 2031. What would you do in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hang on, I suppose. Work every shift. I wouldn't know what else to train in, and I wouldn't trust any course they offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait on the wedding. That breaks my heart, but we couldn't start married life with nothing.

I'm not usually **for rules**, but this is different.
think: I'd lose the warehouse job, and Mark might lose the **sawmill** too.
We'd have **no savings**, no plan and no idea what jobs exist.
do: **Postpone the wedding** until we have some security.
Move back in with **my parents** to cut rent.
Work **every shift** going until the robots come.
feel: **Panicked**, with my heart racing just thinking about it.
S2.quote: We couldn't start married life with nothing.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** and no money, and says so plainly.
She'd **postpone the wedding**, which clearly hurts.
Even her **free-market** views bend: she wants it slowed down.

steps.text: Postpone the church wedding with Mark
Move back in with her parents to save rent
Work every warehouse shift going until robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to be sensible, if folk don't panic. People should look after their own and help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still means losing the warehouse job, around 2034. That's a long way off, but I've got nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry next summer, keep the job, save what I can, maybe 20 a month. And I'd wait a couple of years to see how things go before deciding anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not frozen. There's at least time to pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still marry next summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd marry anyway, small. Family matters more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of savings, Mark still at the sawmill or somewhere else, and maybe a baby. And me with something, anything, that isn't picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, ten years is time to get ready. People should start learning a trade, like in the old days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a long way off for me. By 2039 I'd be nearly 40, with children maybe. I'd worry more about Mark's job than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry, keep the warehouse job and save. Maybe have a baby in a few years. I'd stay where I am unless something pushed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It feels far away, but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Would you plan differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Live my life, work, and see what God sends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about a course at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a cooking course, for a canteen or school kitchen. People will always need feeding.

feel: **Uneasy**, with it far away but still coming.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **live her plans**: marriage, maybe a baby.
Her thin cushion and **certain job loss** keep her anxious despite feeling uneasy.
She considers a **cooking course**, her only retraining idea.

steps.text: Marry and plan a baby in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time, no money and no idea what to do. What would help is family and church, and a company that keeps loyal people on as long as it can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith. A lot of people like me get through hard times with faith, and nobody in these studies ever asks.

portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old picker** at a farm and garden supplies warehouse, slow on the scanner, using paper lists.
She's **engaged to Mark**, who's on short time at the sawmill, with a church wedding planned.
She trusts **family and church** over government, and never uses AI.
Her answer to pressure is to **shrink the wedding**, work harder and pray.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time, no money and no idea what to do.
whatWouldHelp: **Family and church** support to lean on through hard times.
A company that keeps **loyal people** on as long as it can.
